title: Map Tunnel: Dig Straight Through the Earth
description: See where a tunnel straight through the Earth would come out with Map Tunnel — your antipode on the far side of the planet. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, digging from New York lands you in the Indian Ocean southwest of Australia — while digging from Madrid surfaces just off New Zealand, one of the rare land-to-land trips.
quick_answer: Map Tunnel shows the exact point on the opposite side of the Earth from anywhere you pick — the antipode, where a straight tunnel through the planet's centre would emerge. Choose a starting point and watch the second globe answer with the far side's coordinates and country or ocean.

body.t: “Dig to China” is wrong for almost every US kid (the tunnel from most of America surfaces in the Indian Ocean) — and right from Buenos Aires, which faces China across the planet. The
prices the tunnel such a dig implies.
Only a minority of land faces land. Playing the tunnel game across continents rewires a student's sense of the globe faster than any flat map.
Stories that send characters through the Earth owe their readers a real exit point — this page keeps the geography honest.
A small, delighted travel niche visits both a place and its antipode. The tunnel finds the far point; the
dresses its coordinates for the GPS.

Madrid ↔ just off New Zealand's North Island. Quito, Ecuador ↔ Sumatra, Indonesia (land to land). Buenos Aires ↔ off China's coast. New York ↔ empty Indian Ocean. The pairs are the game's high scores.

China's antipodes lie mostly in Argentina and Chile — southern South America is the true 'opposite' of East Asia. From the US, the shovel was always aimed at the ocean; the phrase survives because it is fun, not because it is aimed well.

faq: Does the tunnel pass through the centre?

The straight line between antipodes does — every antipodal tunnel is a diameter. Off-antipode 'tunnels' would be chords shorter than 12,742 km, and this page's pairs are exact opposites by construction.
What place name is shown for ocean exits?
The honest one: open ocean, with the nearest land context where the data supports it. Most of the planet's far sides have no town to name.
Is any city exactly antipodal to another?
None perfectly, but a few are close enough to delight: Madrid and the New Zealand countryside near Weber are within a short drive of true antipody, and Cuenca (Spain) nearly mirrors Hamilton (NZ).
As physics theatre, yes: in a uniform-density, frictionless Earth you would oscillate through in ~42 minutes each way forever. Real rock, heat and pressure file their objections immediately.
Why do both globes move together?
So the pairing stays visceral: drag one side of the planet and the exit point tracks in real time — antipodes are a relationship, not a lookup.
My antipode is near an island — landfall?
If the exit coordinates fall in the sea a few kilometres off a coast, it is an ocean antipode with a view. The coordinate, not the wish, decides.
Can I get the antipode's coordinates as numbers?
Yes — the far point is a normal coordinate pair, copyable into any converter or distance tool on this site.
